Double-Down on Positive Theories The Shift All aspects of organisational analysis: business analysis | enterprise architecture | quality Product Management Product Experimentation Ab Testing The hidden cost of false positives in product experimentation Aram Khachaturyan 3 min read · Oct 13, 2026 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size You pull up your experimentation dashboard, and there it is: a glowing green metric with a p-value under 0.05. Another win for the growth team. Another tiny percentage lift added to the compounding quarterly review deck. Another case study in data-driven optimization. Except, months later, when you check the actual year-end financial statements, the growth isn’t there. Total revenue is flat. You didn’t grow. You just fell victim to the oldest, most pervasive delusion in product management: accidental p-hacking. The Pharmaceutical Trap Imagine a pharmaceutical company that has spent a billion dollars developing a new drug, only to find out it doesn’t work. The company desperately needs FDA approval to recoup its investment. How do they get it? They run clinical trials repeatedly with small cohorts until, purely by random chance, one of the trials happens to hit the 90% confidence threshold. They discard the failed trials, publish the single “successful” result, and get the drug approved. Statisticians call this p-hacking . Because any standard significance test has a built-in false-positive rate (usually 5% or 10%), if you run enough random experiments or peek at your data early, you are mathematically guaranteed to manufacture statistical ghosts. Before you point fingers at drug companies, look at your own product roadmap. Data from enterprise experimentation platforms like Optimizely across thousands of real-world corporate tests reveals a staggering reality: up to 40% of “statistically significant” A/B test wins are false positives. Even elite engineering orgs like Shopify’s growth team find that when they track short-term experiment wins over a 12-month horizon, 35% of those “proven” lifts completely evaporate over time. Why We Fall For It Most product teams don’t p-hack out of malice; they do it because of how we run optimization: The “Shit at the Wall” Strategy: We launch random variations — swapping button colors, rewriting hero copy, tweaking micro-layouts — without an underlying thesis, hoping something will stick. Early Peeking: We check the dashboard every morning. The moment the p-value dips below 0.05, we call the test early, declare victory, and ship it. The Compounding Illusion: We stack twelve “2% wins” over a year, expecting a 26% cumulative lift, only to realize the macro business metrics haven’t moved an inch. When you test random ideas and stop the clock early, you aren’t doing science. You’re just pulling the arm of a slot machine until it rings, and calling it strategy. Moving From Randomness to Validated Learning If you want to stop fooling yourself with statistical noise, you have to change how you approach experimentation: 1. Form a Theory, Don’t Just Test Tactics Stop throwing random variations at the wall. Start with a deep Theory of Customer — a falsifiable hypothesis about why user psychology dictates a specific behavior at a specific moment. If a test fails, a theory gives you something to learn from; a random variation just leaves you guessing. 2. Lock Your Sample Size and Never Peek Calculate your required statistical power and sample size before the test launches based on a meaningful minimum detectable effect. Then, walk away. Let the test run through complete business cycles. If it doesn’t cross the threshold honestly, it’s a loss. Accept it and move on. 3. Double-Down on Positive Theories When an experiment yields a positive result, don’t just ship it and move on. Run an even more extreme variation or extend the theory to adjacent workflows. If the core theory is genuine, the effect will hold or multiply. If the effect disappears, you know you caught a false positive before polluting your codebase. The Shift Data-driven product management is only as honest as your willingness to accept a negative result. When you stop hunting for accidental false positives in dashboard noise and start demanding rigorous, theory-driven validation, your “win rate” will plummet. You will ship fewer features. You will celebrate fewer vanity metrics. But the things that do win will be real. And your business will finally start growing in reality, not just in your analytics deck.
